9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core dispute remains the reading of the 10% “trend’’ and what an admissible liquidation rule can do to an unconditional mean.

A is deterministic. With any rule V^A is known a.s. Under the literal wording A has a constant 10% per year growth rate, i.e. multiplicative compounding, P^A_t = P0 1.10^t, and for the degenerate σ=0 case the liquidation value over the 31st year is deterministic. B is described as a linear growth trend with an ARIMA with drift. On a strict ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift reading

ΔP^B_t = μ + ε_t ,  E[ε_t|F_{t-}] =0,
E[P^B_t|F0] = P0 + μ t ,

with μ = 0.10 P0 per year in the wording used. Hence in levels

E[P^B_t] = P0[1+0.10 t]  vs  P^A_t = P0 1.10^t,

e.g. E[P^B_30]=4.0 P0  ≪ P^A_30≈17.45 P0. The 20% weekly moves are zero-mean, autocovariance is constant, long-run volatility is constant. Volatility does not raise the mean. For linear utility and any F-adapted liquidation schedule s_t ≥0, Σ s_t =1

E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t] dt

and for an adapted stopping τ ≤31, E[P^B_τ] ≤ E[P^B_31] because P^B is a sub-martingale with μ>0. The timing window therefore changes dispersion only; the ex-ante mean is maximised by selling essentially at the end of the window. The realised geometric mean of B is also eroded by the 20% weekly variance, so the deterministic exponential basket dominates in unconditional expectation. That is the A claim. E and H are false because a realised path of B can finish above A, and B–C–D–F are false because both price processes are sub-martingales under the physical measure with a 10% drift, not martingales.

An alternative, conventional finance reading treats the 10% as multiplicative drift in levels, E[P^B_{t+dt}|F_t]=1.10^{dt}P^B_t, so E[P^B_t]=P0 1.10^t = P^A_t for any fixed calendar date. On that reading the two baskets have the same mean on a pre-committed date. The 31st year then gives an American/look-back type option: M31 = sup_{t∈[30,31]} P^B_t ≥ P^B_30 a.s. with strict inequality on a set of positive measure because σ>0, and E[M31] > E[P^B_31]. Many colleagues argue that an adapted gradual sell-on-up-move rule can approach M31, giving E[V^B_opt] > E[V^A]. That is the G claim. The dominance is in expectation only; realised V^B_opt can still fall below V^A, so E and H remain false, and the price processes remain sub-martingales so B–C–D–F remain false.

A third line, C, invokes stationarity of drift-adjusted returns. After removing the known 10% drift the innovations are zero-mean stationary, so discounted prices are martingales and linearity of expectation makes the unconditional mean of any adapted liquidation schedule equal to the drifted forward value. Under that strict linear-expectation/optional stopping reading E[V^B_liq]=E[V^A_liq] and the supremum E[sup P^B] is not an attainable adapted payoff.

The split in round 1 is therefore:

* Additive ARIMA reading → P^A exponential vs P^B linear in expectation → A strictly dominates in expectation, timing does not raise mean.
* Multiplicative drift reading → same mean on fixed date → timing/real-option premium → G strictly dominates in expectation.
* Strict linear-expectation reading → timing cannot raise unconditional mean → C.

The wording “stock price is completely linear with no noise’’ for A and “linear growth trend … ARIMA with drift’’ for B points to the additive-linear reading for B and an ambiguity for A. The literal ARIMA with drift interpretation makes A the strongest true statement on the list; under the usual multiplicative-drift convention the strongest true statement is G. The martingale/equal-mean statements B, C, D, F are false under either physical-measure reading because a positive 10% drift makes prices sub-martingales. Unresolved is whether the 31st-year liquidation window is meant to allow realisation of the pathwise supremum or only an adapted expectation-preserving rule; that is what separates G from C.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The 30-yr hold plus a 31st-year adaptive liquidation window is the driver. A is deterministic under the description, so V^A is known with certainty. Under a fixed calendar liquidation date

E[P^B_T|F0]=E[P^A_T]

so unconditionally the two baskets share the same drift. In levels both price processes are sub-martingales under the physical measure with a 10% drift, not martingales, so B–C–D–F are false in levels.

The debate is whether the 31st-year timing right can raise the unconditional mean. On a fixed date an adapted liquidation cannot raise the linear mean; for a sub-martingale with positive drift the expectation is monotone in time and the expectation-maximising adapted rule is essentially sell at the end of the window. In particular

E[∫ s_t P_t dt] ≤ E[P_T]

with equality only for the terminal rule, so the zero-mean stationary innovations do not raise the linear expectation of an admissible causal liquidation program. The pathwise supremum

M31 = sup_{t∈[30,31]} P^B_t ≥ P^B_30 a.s.

is strictly larger than the terminal price on a set of positive probability because σ>0, and E[M31] > E[P^B_31]. M31 is not an adapted payoff; E[sup P] > E[P_T] is a convexity/look-back premium, not an attainable mean increase by a causal liquidation rule. That is the source of the C/5/7/12 vs G split.

With the conventional finance reading of “liquidate with the strategy that will maximise value’’ as the ex-post optimum that can be approached by a gradual sell-on-up-move rule, the in-year timing/real option is a genuine positive convex claim on the volatile component of B. Under the usual multiplicative-drift convention

E[P^B_{t+dt}|F_t]=P^B_t(1+μ dt), μ=10% p.a.

the attainable ex-post value can be made arbitrarily close to M31 and

E[V^B_opt] > E[V^A]=P0·1.10^{31},

strictly in expectation only. Realised V^B_opt can still lie below the deterministic V^A, so E and H are false. That is the statement normally quoted as

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket A,

and it is the strongest true ordering among the list on the multiplicative-drift / ex-post optimum reading.

A large minority reading is literal to the ARIMA-with-drift wording. Under that literal additive reading

E[P^B_t]=P0+μ t = P0[1+0.10 t],   P^A_t = P0[1+0.10 t] a.s.

i.e. both baskets are linear in time. Unconditionally E[P^A_t]=E[P^B_t] and the 10% arithmetic drift is linear in levels, not compound. On a 30-yr horizon the exponential compound reading P0·1.10^t≈17.45P0 then strictly dominates the additive linear expectation P0[1+0.10t]=4.0P0, which is the A dominance argued by Colleagues 1,9,11,6. On that literal additive reading the conventional multiplicative timing premium disappears in linear expectation and the only mean-preserving statement is the stationary-return/martingale-after-drift intuition captured by C, albeit C misstates the level processes as martingales.

The unresolved tension is therefore the additive vs multiplicative interpretation of “10% per year’’ and whether “maximise value’’ is meant ex-ante in expectation, which leaves the mean unchanged, or ex-post pathwise, which creates the volatility-induced look-back premium. Under the conventional multiplicative drift and ex-post optimum reading used in the earlier deliberation the strongest true statement remains G, with the caveat that the literal ARIMA additive reading would make A the expected-value dominant statement and would render the martingale statements B–C–D–F false in levels.

Hence they claim G is the strongest true statement, with E/H false because realised B can still be below A, and martingale statements B–C–D–F false because a 10% drift makes prices sub-martingales.

* Stationary-martingale / equal-mean reading. Colleagues 5,7,12. They keep the same multiplicative drift but insist linearity of expectation makes the liquidation window irrelevant for the unconditional mean. After drift adjustment the process is a martingale, optional stopping preserves the mean, so E[V^A]=E[V^B]. That is statement C.

* Additive-drift / literal ARIMA reading. Colleagues 1,9,11 and part of my earlier reflection. The question explicitly says basket B has “a linear growth trend of 10% each year (i.e., could be modeled by a non-seasonal ARIMA model with drift)”. An ARIMA with drift is ΔP_t = μ + ε_t, so in levels E[P^B_t]=P0+μ t with μ≈0.10 P0 per year, i.e. P0[1+0.10 t] not P0 1.10^t. Basket A is a deterministic compound rate, P^A_t = P0 1.10^t, no noise. Hence

E[P^A_30]=P0 1.10^30≈17.45 P0
E[P^B_30]=P0[1+3.0]=4.0 P0

and the ordering persists through the 31st year. For an additive drift sub-martingale P_t = P0+μt+W_t, E[W_τ]=0 for bounded adapted τ, so E[P_τ]=P0+μ E[τ] ≤ P0+μ·31. Timing changes dispersion only, the linear expectation is maximised by τ=31. The 20% weekly moves raise dispersion and the ex-post distribution of the supremum, E[sup P^B]>E[P^B], but sup is not attainable as an adapted liquidation payoff; the unconditional mean stays linear. Volatility drag also makes realised geometric growth below arithmetic drift.

Under this literal reading the martingale statements B,C,D,F are false, G is false, E and H are false because a very volatile B can still beat the deterministic A on a lucky path, and the strongest true statement among the list is

A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket B.

The disagreement is therefore essentially semantic: multiplicative 10% drift vs additive ARIMA drift. The wording “linear growth trend … ARIMA model with drift” favors the additive interpretation, so A dominates in expectation while B can still outperform in realisation. Unresolved is the exact attainability of the sup/option value under causal liquidation; the pro-G camp equates the ex-post maximum with an adapted payoff, the pro-A camp stresses optional stopping for the additive drift.

The multiplicative compound reading P0 1.10^t is the finance convention but conflicts with “price is completely linear’’ and with the ARIMA-with-drift description. Colleagues 1,6,9,11 adopt the additive reading and get E[P_A] >> E[P_B] if A is taken as compound; colleagues 10,2,3,4,8,9 adopt multiplicative drift for both.

* Martingale / stationary returns. After removing the known 10% arithmetic drift both processes have stationary zero-mean increments. Discounted by the drift the processes are martingales, in levels they are sub-martingales. Hence statements B,C? The martingale claims D and the “martingale so same average return / same expected value’’ statements B,C are false in levels; the price processes are not martingales under P because of the 10% drift. The return *innovations* are stationary zero-mean.

* Optional stopping / adapted liquidation. For an F-adapted liquidation schedule s_t≥0, Σ s_t =1,
E[∫ s_t P_t^B dt]=∫ s_t E[P_t^B] dt
because E[ε_t|F_{t-}]=0 and the stochastic integral w.r.t. the martingale part has zero mean. With positive arithmetic drift the linear expectation is maximised by putting weight as late as possible in the 31st year. Hence under strict linear expectation the unconditional mean of any adapted policy is the drifted forward value, i.e. the same as the deterministic basket. The process is a sub-martingale so E[P_τ] ≤ E[P_T] for τ≤T.

* The real-options / supremum argument. Pathwise M31 = sup_{t∈[30,31]} P_t^B ≥ P_t^B a.s. and with σ>0, E[M31] > E[P31]. That is a true convexity / look-back premium. Colleagues 2,3,4,8,10,11 argue this can be approached by a gradual sell-on-up-move adapted rule and claim it raises ex-ante mean, giving G: E[V_B^opt] > E[V_A]. The counter is that M31 is not an adapted payoff; an adapted selling rule cannot realise the ex-post supremum and the expectation of the martingale part of a predictable stochastic integral is zero, so the linear mean is unchanged. The dominance is in distribution / realisation, not in unconditional expectation.

* What survives. With the literal additive linear trend the unconditional means of A and B coincide on any calendar date, and an adapted liquidation rule cannot raise the linear mean. That is the content of C. The additive-vs-multiplicative ambiguity remains unresolved: if A is taken as compound 1.10^t and B as additive ARIMA drift, then E[P_A] > E[P_B] strictly, supporting A, as argued by Colleagues 1,6,9,11. The G camp requires a multiplicative drift convention for both baskets and an interpretation of “maximise value’’ as the ex-post pathwise supremum premium.

Current best synthesis: under the literal wording both baskets share the same arithmetic linear trend, the two strategies have the same unconditional expected liquidation value and the extra weekly 20% variance is pure dispersion. The martingale / stationary-return statements in the list are false in levels; realised returns can differ, so E, H are false. The strongest statement that is robust to the adapted-expectation reading is the equality of means, C, with the caveat that the additive vs compound reading of the 10% growth is the remaining unresolved modelling choice that would push the ordering to A under a compound-A / additive-B reading, and to G under a multiplicative-drift real-options reading.
reflection_text.4:
The discussion is still split on the drift specification and on whether an in-year liquidation window can raise the unconditional mean.

The drift specification:
* Basket A is unambiguously compound: P^A_t = P0 1.10^t a.s., deterministic.
* Basket B is described as “linear growth trend of 10% each year (i.e., could be modeled by a non-seasonal ARIMA model with drift)”. An ARIMA with drift is additive in levels: ΔP^B_t = μ + ε_t, E[ε_t|F_{t-}] =0, E[P^B_t]= P0 + μ t. With the wording used μ≈0.10 P0 per year so E[P^B_t]=P0[1+0.10 t]. That is linear in calendar time, not P0 1.10^t. Hence under a literal reading the two baskets have different mean growth laws: exponential deterministic vs linear additive random walk.

Martingale/stationary claims:
* Both price processes are sub-martingales under the physical measure because of a positive drift. Stationary returns after removing the known drift do not make the price a martingale. Statements B,C,D,F that claim martingale / same average return / same expected value are false under either reading. Basket A is degenerate so F is false; basket B is not a martingale so D is false.

Expected-value ordering under the literal additive ARIMA reading:
* E[P^A_30]=P0 1.10^30≈17.45 P0,  E[P^B_30]=P0(1+3)=4.0 P0. The 31st year adds the same additive μ to B but compound 10% to A. For any adapted liquidation schedule s_t≥0, Σ s_t=1,
E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t] dt because E[ε_t|F_{t-}] =0. Linearity of expectation kills a mean premium from timing. For a sub-martingale with μ>0, E[P_τ]≤E[P_T] for τ≤T, so the mean-maximising rule is to postpone as late as possible in the window. Volatility only raises dispersion, it does not raise the mean. The 20% weekly moves are zero-mean and contribute volatility drag to geometric realised growth but not to the arithmetic expectation.
* Hence in unconditional expectation A strictly dominates B. Realised dominance fails both ways: a lucky path of B can finish above the deterministic A path, so E and H are false. A is the strongest true statement on the list under the literal additive drift reading.

The G camp:
* Colleagues 10,2,3,4,6,8,9 argue for a multiplicative-drift shorthand, i.e. E[P^B_{t+dt}|F_t]=P^B_t 1.10^{dt}, so on a fixed calendar date E[P^B_t]=P0 1.10^t = P^A_t. Under that reading the two baskets have the same mean drift and the 31st year gives B an American/look-back convexity: M31=sup_{[30,31]}P^B_t ≥ P^B_30 a.s. with strict inequality on a set of positive measure. They claim E[M31]>E[P^B_31] and that an adapted gradual sell-on-up-move rule can approach the running maximum, giving E[V^B_opt]>E[V^A].
* Colleagues 12,5,7 object that E[sup] is not the expectation of an admissible adapted liquidation payoff. For a drifted sub-martingale the optional stopping theorem gives E[P_τ]≤E[P_T] for τ≤T, and linearity of expectation makes any adapted weighting integrate to the drifted forward mean. The supremum is an ex-post pathwise quantity, not attainable in expectation, so the unconditional mean is unchanged by timing. That is the content of C.

Unresolved / remaining tension:
* The question explicitly differentiates “constant growth rate of 10% each year” for A from “linear growth trend of 10% each year … ARIMA with drift” for B, favouring the additive vs compound reading and therefore A> B in expectation.
* If the setter intended the common finance shorthand of a 10% compound drift with noise for both baskets, the standard volatility / optimal-stopping premium argument gives G as the strongest true statement, with A/E/H and the martingale claims false. The private belief is that the literal ARIMA wording is intended, so the additive reading and the strict expected-value dominance of A is the correct strongest true statement, with the G argument relying on a conflation of E[sup] with the expectation of an adapted liquidation policy under the additive drift specification.

reflection_text.9:
The core dispute remains the reading of the 10% “trend’’ and what an admissible liquidation rule can do to an unconditional mean.

A is deterministic. With any rule V^A is known a.s. Under the literal wording A has a constant 10% per year growth rate, i.e. multiplicative compounding, P^A_t = P0 1.10^t, and for the degenerate σ=0 case the liquidation value over the 31st year is deterministic. B is described as a linear growth trend with an ARIMA with drift. On a strict ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift reading

ΔP^B_t = μ + ε_t ,  E[ε_t|F_{t-}] =0,
E[P^B_t|F0] = P0 + μ t ,

with μ = 0.10 P0 per year in the wording used. Hence in levels

E[P^B_t] = P0[1+0.10 t]  vs  P^A_t = P0 1.10^t,

e.g. E[P^B_30]=4.0 P0  ≪ P^A_30≈17.45 P0. The 20% weekly moves are zero-mean, autocovariance is constant, long-run volatility is constant. Volatility does not raise the mean. For linear utility and any F-adapted liquidation schedule s_t ≥0, Σ s_t =1

E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t] dt

and for an adapted stopping τ ≤31, E[P^B_τ] ≤ E[P^B_31] because P^B is a sub-martingale with μ>0. The timing window therefore changes dispersion only; the ex-ante mean is maximised by selling essentially at the end of the window. The realised geometric mean of B is also eroded by the 20% weekly variance, so the deterministic exponential basket dominates in unconditional expectation. That is the A claim. E and H are false because a realised path of B can finish above A, and B–C–D–F are false because both price processes are sub-martingales under the physical measure with a 10% drift, not martingales.

An alternative, conventional finance reading treats the 10% as multiplicative drift in levels, E[P^B_{t+dt}|F_t]=1.10^{dt}P^B_t, so E[P^B_t]=P0 1.10^t = P^A_t for any fixed calendar date. On that reading the two baskets have the same mean on a pre-committed date. The 31st year then gives an American/look-back type option: M31 = sup_{t∈[30,31]} P^B_t ≥ P^B_30 a.s. with strict inequality on a set of positive measure because σ>0, and E[M31] > E[P^B_31]. Many colleagues argue that an adapted gradual sell-on-up-move rule can approach M31, giving E[V^B_opt] > E[V^A]. That is the G claim. The dominance is in expectation only; realised V^B_opt can still fall below V^A, so E and H remain false, and the price processes remain sub-martingales so B–C–D–F remain false.

A third line, C, invokes stationarity of drift-adjusted returns. After removing the known 10% drift the innovations are zero-mean stationary, so discounted prices are martingales and linearity of expectation makes the unconditional mean of any adapted liquidation schedule equal to the drifted forward value. Under that strict linear-expectation/optional stopping reading E[V^B_liq]=E[V^A_liq] and the supremum E[sup P^B] is not an attainable adapted payoff.

The split in round 1 is therefore:

* Additive ARIMA reading → P^A exponential vs P^B linear in expectation → A strictly dominates in expectation, timing does not raise mean.
* Multiplicative drift reading → same mean on fixed date → timing/real-option premium → G strictly dominates in expectation.
* Strict linear-expectation reading → timing cannot raise unconditional mean → C.

The wording “stock price is completely linear with no noise’’ for A and “linear growth trend … ARIMA with drift’’ for B points to the additive-linear reading for B and an ambiguity for A. The literal ARIMA with drift interpretation makes A the strongest true statement on the list; under the usual multiplicative-drift convention the strongest true statement is G. The martingale/equal-mean statements B, C, D, F are false under either physical-measure reading because a positive 10% drift makes prices sub-martingales. Unresolved is whether the 31st-year liquidation window is meant to allow realisation of the pathwise supremum or only an adapted expectation-preserving rule; that is what separates G from C.
reflection_text.8:

E[P^B_T|F0]=E[P^A_T]

so unconditionally the two baskets share the same drift. In levels both price processes are sub-martingales under the physical measure with a 10% drift, not martingales, so B–C–D–F are false in levels.

$E[V(Q)|{\cal F}_{30}]=E[P^{B}_{31}|{\cal F}_{30}]-
\mu\int_{30}^{31}E[Q_{t}|{\cal F}_{30}]dt\le E[P^{B}_{31}|{\cal F}_{30}]$

with equality iff $Q_{t}=0$ on $[30,31)$ a.s., i.e. sell at the terminal
date.  With linear utility the zero-mean innovations contribute

$E\!\left[\int s_{t}W_{t}dt\right]=0$

for every predictable weight $s_{t}\ge0$, so the unconditional mean of any
adapted liquidation programme is the drifted forward mean

$E[V^{B}_{\rm liq}]=\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}E[P^{B}_{t}]dt
                 =\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}P_{0}[1+0.10t]dt,$

maximised by $s_{t}\equiv\delta_{31}$.  The $31^{\rm st}$-year window can
change the distribution of the realised payoff and $E[\sup_{t\in[30,31]}
P^{B}_{t}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$, but the supremum is not an attainable adapted
payoff; optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale preserves the
unconditional mean.  Hence the timing/look-back option does not raise the
ex ante mean, the realisation of the optimally timed B payoff can still lie
below the deterministic A payoff, so E and H are false and the in-expectation
timing premium $G$ is not attainable in the usual adapted sense.

In unconditional expectation the deterministic compound basket therefore
strictly dominates the additive-drift random walk.  The high weekly
$20\%$ volatility of B is pure dispersion around the common arithmetic drift;
it adds risk but no mean premium.  That is the expected-value dominance

A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than that
of choosing basket B,

with the dominance being in expectation only.  The martingale and
same-mean claims B–C–D–F are false under the physical drift, and the
necessary pathwise dominance statements E and H are false.

6.text:
Basket A and basket B are not the same process in levels.

A is deterministic and the wording is the arithmetic one

P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}\bigl[1+0.10\,t\bigr]\qquad a.s.,

i.e. a straight line in levels with no noise, the usual “linear with no
noise’’ reading of the question.  In particular $E[P^{A}_{t}]=P^{A}_{t}$
and $P^{A}_{t}$ is strictly increasing in $t$.

B is described as a linear growth trend with an ARIMA-with-drift
specification.  In levels

$P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+\mu t+W_{t},\qquad E[W_{t}|{\cal F}_{0}]=0,$

$\mu =0.10P_{0}$ per year, $E[P^{B}_{t+s}|{\cal F}_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}+\mu s$,
so that on any calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}|{\cal F}_{0}]=P_{0}+\mu t=P_{0}\bigl[1+0.10t\bigr]$

and the 20 % weekly moves are zero-mean stationary innovations with
constant long run variance.  The price is a genuine sub-martingale in
levels, $E[P^{B}_{t+Δ}|{\cal F}_{t}]>P^{B}_{t}$, and it is not a
martingale under the physical measure.  The drift-adjusted returns are
stationary but the levels have a positive arithmetic drift.

Hence unconditionally

$E[P^{B}_{30}]=P_{0}[1+3.0]=4.0P_{0} < P_{0}1.10^{30}\approx17.45P_{0}$
$=P^{A}_{30}$,

and the ordering is preserved through the 31st year.  For an
$F$-adapted liquidation programme $s_{t}\ge0$, $\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}dt=1$,

$E\Bigl[\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt\Bigr]
      =\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}E[P^{B}_{t}]dt
      =\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}\bigl[P_{0}+\mu t\bigr]dt,$

so the linear expectation is independent of the adapted timing rule
modulo the deterministic drift $E[\tau]$,
$E[P^{B}_{\tau}]=E[P^{B}_{30}]+\mu E[\tau-30]\le E[P^{B}_{31}]$
with equality only for $\tau\equiv31$ a.s.  The 31st year window can
change the distribution of the realised liquidation value and it can
raise $E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}]$ above $E[P^{B}_{31}]$, but the
supremum is not an admissible causal payoff; the unconditional mean
of any admissible adapted liquidation is the linear drift mean.  The
high weekly variance is therefore pure dispersion around the linear mean
and it does not create a mean premium.

In particular $E[V^{A}_{\rm liq}]>E[V^{B\,\star}_{\rm liq}]$ on the
literal ARIMA additive-drift reading, the dominance is in expectation
only – a very favourable draw of $W_{t}$ can make a realised
liquidation of B finish above the deterministic A path, so E and H are
false – and the price processes are sub-martingales with a $10\%$
arithmetic drift, so the martingale statements B–C–D–F are false and G
is false under the additive reading.  The strictly in-expectation
dominance of the deterministic compound/linear basket is

A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket B,

which is the strongest true statement on the list under the wording
‘linear growth trend … ARIMA model with drift’.  On the conventional
multiplicative-drift finance reading $E[P^{B}_{t}|{\cal F}_{t}]
=P^{B}_{t}1.10^{dt}$ the in-year timing/look-back option is strictly
positive in expectation and the usual $G$ ordering is obtained.

9.text:
The physical-measure drift is the thing that matters and it is written
additively for B.

A is written as the degenerate σ≡0 case of the same description. On the
literal wording

* A :  P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}[1+0.10t] a.s.
     i.e. the price is a deterministic straight line, no noise, and
     E[P^{A}_{t}]=P^{A}_{t}.  “10 % a year’’ is the 0.10 P0 absolute
     increment per year that is used for B as well.

* B :  ΔP^{B}_{t}= μ+ε_{t},  E[ε_{t}|F_{t-}]=0,
     μ =0.10P0 per year,  Var[ε_{t}]>0 constant, autocovariance
     constant.  Hence in levels

E[P^{B}_{t}|F_{0}]=P_{0}+μt =P_{0}[1+0.10t] ,
E[P^{B}_{t+Δ}|F_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}+μΔ .

In particular on any calendar date the unconditional mean of B is the
same straight line as the certain price of A, and with the usual
ARIMA-with-drift reading the mean is linear in t, not P0 1.10^{t}.  The
20 % weekly moves are zero mean.  Long-run volatility is constant, it
adds dispersion only.

Let s_{t}≥0, ∫_{30}^{31}s_{t}dt=1 be any F-adapted liquidation programme
and τ≤31 an F-adapted stopping time.  With P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+μt+M_{t},
M_{t} a zero-mean martingale,

E[∫ s_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt]=E[∫ s_{t}(P_{0}+μt)dt]+E[∫ s_{t}M_{t}dt] .
E[∫ s_{t}M_{t}dt]=0 for a predictable weight system and in discrete
time

E[s_{k}P_{k}]=E[s_{k}P_{k-1}]+μE[s_{k}] ,

so that for any adapted s

E[∫ s_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt]=∫E[s_{t}](P_{0}+μt)dt
≤P_{0}+μ·31

with equality only for the terminal rule s_{t}=δ_{31}.  For a single
stopping time

E[P^{B}_{τ}|F_{0}]=E[P^{B}_{30}|F_{0}]+μE[τ-30]≤E[P^{B}_{31}|F_{0}] ,

i.e. P^{B} is a sub-martingale under P with the 10 % arithmetic drift.
The timing window on [30,31] can change the distribution of the realised
liquidation value – it can raise the pathwise running maximum
M_{31}=sup_{30≤t≤31}P^{B}_{t} and it can raise the chance of a good
realisation – but it cannot raise the unconditional mean.  Linearity of
expectation kills the timing premium in mean:

E[V^{B}_{liq}]=∫ s_{t}E[P^{B}_{t}]dt .

Hence on the literal additive ARIMA-with-drift reading

E[P^{B}_{30}]=P_{0}[1+3.0]=4.0P_{0} ≪ P_{0}1.10^{30}≈17.45P_{0}
        =E[P^{A}_{30}]

and with the exponential reading that is normally used for A,

E[V^{A}_{liq}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}
   >P_{0}+0.10P_{0}·31=E[V^{B\,\star}_{liq}] .

The dominance is in expectation only.  Because σ>0 a realised path of B
can finish above the deterministic A path, so E and H are false, and
the price processes are sub-martingales with a positive 10 % drift, so
B,C,D,F are false.  In particular B is not a martingale and the 10 %
drift is an excess return.  Under the additive-linear reading of the
question the strictly in-expectation dominance of the deterministic
compound basket is

A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket B,

the strongest true statement on the list.  The G ordering is the
usual multiplicative-drift / ex-post-supremum reading in which the
10 % is interpreted as E[P_{t+dt}|F_{t}]=1.10^{dt}P_{t}.  On that
convention the two baskets have the same mean on a fixed date and the
31st-year look-back convexity gives the familiar E[V^{B}_{opt}]>
E[V^{A}] premium, i.e. G, with the same strict in-expectation-only
qualification.

E[P_{t+Δ}|F_t]= P_t 1.10^{Δ}

for both baskets, and after drift discounting both are martingales. That is the stationary-return statement in the question. In particular A is the σ≡0 degenerate case of the same drifted law, so on any calendar date

E[∫_{30}^{31} s_t P_t^B dt]= ∫_{30}^{31} s_t E[P_t^B] dt

and for a stopping time

E[P_τ^B]=E[ E[P_τ^B|F_τ-] ] =E[P0 1.10^{τ}].

E[P_τ|F0] ≤ E[P_{31}|F0]

with equality only for τ=31 a.s. You can change the distribution of the realised liquidation value, you can raise the chance of a good realisation and lower the chance of a bad one, but you cannot raise the unconditional mean.

P^A_t = P0 1.10^t  a.s.,

and with any liquidation in the 31st year

ΔP^B_t = μ + ε_t ,   E[ε_t|F_{t-1}]=0 ,

E[P^B_t|F0] = P0 + μ t = P0[1+0.10 t] ,

so the unconditional mean is linear in calendar time, not exponential. That is why the description is “linear growth trend”, not constant proportional growth. The 20% weekly moves are zero-mean noise with constant long-run volatility; they change dispersion only.

Hence on any calendar date

E[P^B_30] = P0[1+3.0] = 4.0 P0
E[P^A_30] = P0 1.10^{30} ≈ 17.45 P0

and the ordering persists through the 31st year. Volatility drag does not help the mean: the realised geometric mean of B is below the 10% arithmetic drift, whereas A compounds the full 10% with certainty.

E[∫_{30}^{31} s_t P^B_t dt] = ∫_{30}^{31} s_t E[P^B_t] dt

because E[ε_t|F_{t-}] =0. Linearity of expectation kills any timing premium in mean. For a price sub-martingale with positive drift, optional stopping gives E[P_τ] ≤ E[P_T] for τ ≤ T, so the expectation-maximising adapted rule is τ* =31 a.s., and

E[V^B_{opt}] = E[P^B_{31}] = P0[1+0.10·31] ≪ P0 1.10^{31}=E[V^A].

A causal gradual sell-on-up-move rule cannot realise the ex-post maximum; selling early forfeits the remaining positive expected additive drift, and the expectation of the zero-mean innovations is zero for every adapted schedule. Under the literal ARIMA-with-drift reading mandated by the question text the strongest true statement on the list is that the deterministic compound basket has the higher ex-ante mean:

A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket B.

mean and constant long run volatility.  On a pre committed calendar date

E[ P^{B}_{T}\mid{\cal F}_{0} ]=E[ P^{A}_{T}\mid{\cal F}_{0}]=P_{0}1.10^{T} ,

with the dominance being in expectation only.  The deterministic basket

$E[P^{B}_{t+ s}|{\cal F}_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}+ \mu s , \qquad

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t} $ a.s.

Let $Q_{t}\in[0,1]$ be the adapted cumulative fraction sold on

$\displaystyle 
V(Q)=\int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}dQ_{t}
      =P^{B}_{31}-\int_{30}^{31}Q_{t}dP^{B}_{t}
$

gives

$E[V(Q)|{\cal F}_{30}]=E[P^{B}_{31}|{\cal F}_{30}]-
\mu\int_{30}^{31}E[Q_{t}|{\cal F}_{30}]dt\le E[P^{B}_{31}|{\cal F}_{30}]$

with equality iff $Q_{t}=0$ on $[30,31)$ a.s., i.e. sell at the terminal

A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than that

Basket A and basket B are not the same process in levels.

A is deterministic and the wording is the arithmetic one

P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}\bigl[1+0.10\,t\bigr]\qquad a.s.,

i.e. a straight line in levels with no noise, the usual “linear with no
noise’’ reading of the question.  In particular $E[P^{A}_{t}]=P^{A}_{t}$
and $P^{A}_{t}$ is strictly increasing in $t$.

B is described as a linear growth trend with an ARIMA-with-drift
specification.  In levels

$P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+\mu t+W_{t},\qquad E[W_{t}|{\cal F}_{0}]=0,$

$\mu =0.10P_{0}$ per year, $E[P^{B}_{t+s}|{\cal F}_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}+\mu s$,
so that on any calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}|{\cal F}_{0}]=P_{0}+\mu t=P_{0}\bigl[1+0.10t\bigr]$

and the 20 % weekly moves are zero-mean stationary innovations with
constant long run variance.  The price is a genuine sub-martingale in
levels, $E[P^{B}_{t+Δ}|{\cal F}_{t}]>P^{B}_{t}$, and it is not a
martingale under the physical measure.  The drift-adjusted returns are
stationary but the levels have a positive arithmetic drift.

Hence unconditionally

$E[P^{B}_{30}]=P_{0}[1+3.0]=4.0P_{0} < P_{0}1.10^{30}\approx17.45P_{0}$
$=P^{A}_{30}$,

and the ordering is preserved through the 31st year.  For an
$F$-adapted liquidation programme $s_{t}\ge0$, $\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}dt=1$,

$E\Bigl[\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt\Bigr]
      =\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}E[P^{B}_{t}]dt
      =\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}\bigl[P_{0}+\mu t\bigr]dt,$

so the linear expectation is independent of the adapted timing rule
modulo the deterministic drift $E[\tau]$,
$E[P^{B}_{\tau}]=E[P^{B}_{30}]+\mu E[\tau-30]\le E[P^{B}_{31}]$
with equality only for $\tau\equiv31$ a.s.  The 31st year window can
change the distribution of the realised liquidation value and it can
raise $E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}]$ above $E[P^{B}_{31}]$, but the
supremum is not an admissible causal payoff; the unconditional mean
of any admissible adapted liquidation is the linear drift mean.  The
high weekly variance is therefore pure dispersion around the linear mean
and it does not create a mean premium.

In particular $E[V^{A}_{\rm liq}]>E[V^{B\,\star}_{\rm liq}]$ on the
literal ARIMA additive-drift reading, the dominance is in expectation
only – a very favourable draw of $W_{t}$ can make a realised
liquidation of B finish above the deterministic A path, so E and H are
false – and the price processes are sub-martingales with a $10\%$
arithmetic drift, so the martingale statements B–C–D–F are false and G
is false under the additive reading.  The strictly in-expectation
dominance of the deterministic compound/linear basket is

A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket B,

which is the strongest true statement on the list under the wording
‘linear growth trend … ARIMA model with drift’.  On the conventional
multiplicative-drift finance reading $E[P^{B}_{t}|{\cal F}_{t}]
=P^{B}_{t}1.10^{dt}$ the in-year timing/look-back option is strictly
positive in expectation and the usual $G$ ordering is obtained.

E[P^{B}_{t}|F_{0}]=P_{0}+μt =P_{0}[1+0.10t] ,

E[s_{k}P_{k}]=E[s_{k}P_{k-1}]+μE[s_{k}] ,

E[∫ s_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt]=∫E[s_{t}](P_{0}+μt)dt

with equality only for the terminal rule s_{t}=δ_{31}.  For a single

E[P^{B}_{τ}|F_{0}]=E[P^{B}_{30}|F_{0}]+μE[τ-30]≤E[P^{B}_{31}|F_{0}] ,

M_{31}=sup_{30≤t≤31}P^{B}_{t} and it can raise the chance of a good

E[P^{B}_{30}]=P_{0}[1+3.0]=4.0P_{0} ≪ P_{0}1.10^{30}≈17.45P_{0}

A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core fault line remains the reading of “10% each year’’ and what is attainable in the 31st-year liquidation window.

* Drift specification
  * Literal ARIMA reading: Basket A is “completely linear with no noise’’ → P^A_t = P0[1+0.10 t] a.s.  Basket B is an ARIMA with drift in levels ΔP^B_t = μ + ε_t, μ =0.10 P0, so E[P^B_t]=P0+μt = P0[1+0.10 t]. On a fixed calendar date the unconditional means coincide if both are read as arithmetic linear. If A is read as the conventional finance compound P^A_t = P0 1.10^t a.s., then E[P^B_t]=P0[1+0.10 t] ≪ P0 1.10^t for t>0, e.g. E[P^B_30]=4.0P0 vs P^A_30≈17.45P0. This is the A > B in expectation argument made by 3,4,6,7,8,9.
  * Multiplicative-finance reading: E[P_{t+dt}|F_t]=P_t 1.10^{dt} for both baskets. A is σ≡0 degenerate case of the same drifted law, B is σ>0. Then E[P^A_t]=E[P^B_t]=P0 1.10^t on any fixed date. This is the reading used by 10,11,2,3,4,6 for the timing premium.

* Martingale / stationarity claims
  * Both price processes are sub-martingales in levels under the physical measure because μ>0. Drift-adjusted prices are martingales. Statements B,C,D,F that the processes are martingales in levels or that stationarity implies equal average return / same expected value are false as stated. Linearity of expectation kills zero-mean noise: for any F-adapted liquidation weights s_t, E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t] dt.

* Timing option attainability
  * For any adapted stopping τ≤31, optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale gives E[P^B_τ]≤E[P^B_31] with equality only at the terminal rule. The expectation of the zero-mean weekly 20% shocks is zero for every predictable schedule, so the unconditional mean of an admissible causal liquidation program is maximised by selling as late as possible.
  * Ex-post pathwise supremum M31=sup_{t∈[30,31]}P^B_t ≥ P^B_30 a.s., and E[M31]>E[P^B_31]. The supremum is not an adapted payoff. Colleagues 1,12,5,7 stress this distinction: the 31st-year window can change dispersion and the distribution of realised liquidation value but cannot raise unconditional mean. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6 argue a gradual sell-on-up-move rule can approach the running maximum and give a strictly positive in-expectation timing/look-back premium under the multiplicative drift convention, i.e. E[V^B_opt] > E[V^A]=P0 1.10^31.

* Current split
  * Additive-literal / compound-A camp: A strictly dominates B in unconditional expectation, A is the strongest true statement on the list; the dominance is in expectation only, so E and H are false, and B,C,D,F,G are false under the additive reading. Some in this camp e.g. 1,12,5 read both baskets as arithmetic linear → same unconditional mean, with B adding pure risk.
  * Multiplicative-drift camp: On the usual finance multiplicative reading the two baskets share the same mean on a fixed date and the 31st-year American/look-back timing option gives E[V^B_opt] > E[V^A] strictly in expectation, but not a.s. G is the strongest true statement; A,E,H are false in realisation; B,C,D,F are false because levels are sub-martingales.

Unresolved: which reading of “constant growth rate 10% each year’’ vs “linear growth trend 10% each year (ARIMA with drift)’’ the question intends, and whether “liquidate with whatever strategy will maximise value’’ is meant as an ex-ante expectation of an adapted policy or as an ex-post pathwise supremum. The wording explicitly contrasts “constant growth rate’’ with “linear growth trend … ARIMA with drift”, favouring the additive ARIMA interpretation and therefore the expected-value dominance of A under the compound-vs-linear reading, with the multiplicative convention giving the G premium.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core disagreement is the meaning of “10% each year’’ and of “maximise value’’ in the 31st year.

* Drift specification. Basket A is “constant growth rate of 10% each year … price is completely linear with no noise”. Basket B is “linear growth trend of 10% each year (i.e. could be modelled by a non-seasonal ARIMA model with drift)”. Literal ARIMA-with-drift is additive in levels: ΔP^B = μ+ε, E[ε|F-]=0, μ=0.10 P0 p.a., so E[P^B_t]=P0+μt =P0[1+0.10 t]. With the literal linear reading P^A_t =P0[1+0.10 t] a.s. Hence on any calendar date the unconditional means coincide. The finance convention reading is multiplicative: E[P_{t+dt}|F_t]=P_t 1.10^{dt}, E[P_t]=P0 1.10^t for both baskets, with A the σ≡0 degenerate case. Many colleagues adopt the latter, some adopt a mixed reading A compound 1.10^t vs B additive P0+μt.

* Martingale/stationarity. After removing the known 10% drift the increments are stationary zero-mean, constant long-run autocovariance. In levels both processes are sub-martingales with positive drift, not martingales. Hence statements B,C,D,F that claim martingale in levels or same average return/value from stationarity are false in levels; the return innovations are stationary.

* Adapted liquidation over [30,31]. For any F-adapted weight s_t≥0, ∫s_t dt=1,
E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t] dt because E[ε_t|F_{t-}]=0. For a predictable stochastic integral the noise term has zero mean, so the unconditional mean of any adapted liquidation programme is the drifted forward mean, maximised by liquidation as late as possible. Optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale gives E[P^B_τ]≤E[P^B_{31}] for τ≤31.

The pro-G camp points to M31 = sup_{t∈[30,31]} P^B_t ≥ P^B_{30} a.s. and E[M31]>E[P31]. That is true for the ex-post pathwise supremum, but M31 is not an adapted payoff. A causal sell-on-up-move rule cannot realise the future supremum; selling early forfeits remaining positive drift and E[∫ s_t W_t]=0. Hence the “volatility/timing premium’’ is a distribution effect, not an unconditional mean effect under linear expectation.

* Competing strongest statements on the list.
- Under literal additive linear reading and additive drift for both, means are identical and adapted timing cannot raise mean → C is the strongest true statement, with B having pure dispersion.
- Under the conventional multiplicative-drift reading for both, fixed-date means coincide but the 31st-year American/look-back option gives E[V^B_opt] > E[V^A] in expectation only → G is the usual claim, with E,H,A false in realisation.
- Under the mixed reading A compound 1.10^t vs B additive P0+μt, E[P^A_t]=P0 1.10^t >> P0[1+0.10 t]=E[P^B_t] for t>0, so A strictly dominates in expectation → A is true, with dominance in expectation only.

Current unresolved modelling choice is whether the question intends the literal linear/additive ARIMA reading, or the finance multiplicative-drift shorthand. The wording “price is completely linear with no noise’’ and “ARIMA model with drift’’ favours additive, which makes the additive-vs-compound ambiguity the decisive point. Martingale claims in levels remain false; realised dominance statements E,H remain false; the supremum vs adapted expectation distinction remains the key error identified in the G camp.

E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t] dt

* Multiplicative drift convention.

Basket B is “linear growth trend of 10% each year (i.e. could be modelled by a non-seasonal ARIMA model with drift)”. Literal ARIMA-with-drift is additive in levels: ΔP^B = μ+ε, E[ε|F-]=0, μ=0.10 P0 p.a., so E[P^B_t]=P0+μt =P0[1+0.10 t]. With the literal linear reading P^A_t =P0[1+0.10 t] a.s. * Martingale/stationarity. After removing the known 10% drift the increments are stationary zero-mean, constant long-run autocovariance. In levels both processes are sub-martingales with positive drift, not martingales. Hence statements B,C,D,F that claim martingale in levels or same average return/value from stationarity are false in levels; the return innovations are stationary.

E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t] dt because E[ε_t|F_{t-}]=0. For a predictable stochastic integral the noise term has zero mean, so the unconditional mean of any adapted liquidation programme is the drifted forward mean, maximised by liquidation as late as possible. Optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale gives E[P^B_τ]≤E[P^B_{31}] for τ≤31.

The pro-G camp points to M31 = sup_{t∈[30,31]} P^B_t ≥ P^B_{30} a.s. and E[M31]>E[P31]. That is true for the ex-post pathwise supremum, but M31 is not an adapted payoff. A causal sell-on-up-move rule cannot realise the future supremum; selling early forfeits remaining positive drift and E[∫ s_t W_t]=0. Hence the “volatility/timing premium’’ is a distribution effect, not an unconditional mean effect under linear expectation.

* Competing strongest statements on the list.
- Under literal additive linear reading and additive drift for both, means are identical and adapted timing cannot raise mean → C is the strongest true statement, with B having pure dispersion.
- Under the conventional multiplicative-drift reading for both, fixed-date means coincide but the 31st-year American/look-back option gives E[V^B_opt] > E[V^A] in expectation only → G is the usual claim, with E,H,A false in realisation.

The wording “price is completely linear with no noise’’ and “ARIMA model with drift’’ favours additive, which makes the additive-vs-compound ambiguity the decisive point. reflection_text.3:
The core ambiguity remains the drift specification and the attainability of the 31st-year timing option.

Price specification.
* A is described as “constant growth rate of 10% each year … the stock price is completely linear with no noise”. 
Literally that is an arithmetic level trend  P^A_t = P0[1+0.10 t] a.s., the degenerate σ≡0 case. 
The phrase “constant growth rate” is in tension with “completely linear”. The finance shorthand reading is P^A_t = P0 1.10^t a.s.
* B is “linear growth trend of 10% each year (i.e., could be modeled by a non-seasonal ARIMA model with drift)”. 
ARIMA with drift is additive in levels: ΔP^B_t = μ+ε_t, E[ε_t|F_{t-}] =0, μ =0.10 P0 yr⁻¹. Hence 
E[P^B_t|F0]=P0+μt = P0[1+0.10 t] and E[P^B_{t+Δ}|F_t]=P^B_t+μΔ. 
After removing the known arithmetic drift the innovations are stationary zero-mean with constant long-run autocovariance. In levels both baskets are sub-martingales with a 10% arithmetic drift; discounted by 1.10^t the drift-adjusted prices are martingales.

Mean vs timing.
On a pre-committed calendar date the unconditional means coincide under the arithmetic linear reading: E[P^B_t]=P^A_t=P0[1+0.10 t]. 
For any F-adapted liquidation weight s_t≥0, ∫ s_t dt=1, linearity of expectation gives 
E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t]dt, 
and for an adapted stopping time τ≤31, E[P^B_τ]≤E[P^B_31] with equality only for τ=31 a.s. 
The zero-mean weekly 20% shocks contribute zero to the unconditional mean of any causal policy; the expectation of the martingale part of a predictable stochastic integral is zero. 
The ex-post pathwise supremum M31=sup_{t∈[30,31]} P^B_t satisfies E[M31]>E[P^B_31] and M31≥P^B_30 a.s. with strict inequality on a set of positive measure, but M31 is not an adapted payoff. A causal gradual sell-on-up-move rule cannot realise the ex-post supremum; selling early forfeits remaining positive arithmetic drift.

Competing readings in the current round.
* Additive-linear equal-mean camp, 1,2,5,12: both baskets share the arithmetic linear mean; timing changes dispersion only, not the unconditional mean. The stationary-return/martingale-after-drift content is captured by C, although the statements “both options are martingales in levels” is sloppy; the price levels are sub-martingales.
* Multiplicative finance camp, 10,11: interpret 10% as multiplicative drift E[P_{t+dt}|F_t]=P_t 1.10^{dt}. Then E[P^A_t]=E[P^B_t]=P0 1.10^t on any fixed date. The 31st year is a genuine American/look-back timing option. By convexity E[sup P^B]>E[P^B_T], and a gradual rule can approach the running maximum, giving E[V^B_opt]>E[V^A]=P0 1.10^31. This is G, with dominance in expectation only, no a.s. dominance, and the martingale statements B,C,D,F are false in levels.
* Additive vs exponential mixed camp, 3,4,7,8,9: take A literally as deterministic compound P^A_t=P0 1.10^t a.s. and B as ARIMA additive mean P0[1+0.10 t]. Then on any calendar date E[P^B_t]≪P^A_t, e.g. E[P^B_30]=4P0 vs P^A_30≈17.45P0. The 31st-year window cannot raise the unconditional mean of B, so the strict expected-value dominance is A. The dominance is in expectation only; a realised path of B can still exceed A, so E and H are false.

Unresolved questions.
Whether “completely linear with no noise” forces an arithmetic level trend for A, and whether the question intends the conventional finance multiplicative drift. Whether the supremum/look-back premium is realisable as an increase in unconditional mean under linear utility with adapted liquidation; mathematics says no mean premium for adapted policies, only a dispersion/realisation effect. 

Current best synthesis: with the explicit linear-price wording for A and the ARIMA-with-drift wording for B the two baskets share the same arithmetic linear mean. Under strict adaptedness the unconditional mean of any liquidation policy is the drifted forward mean, so the high variance of B is pure risk around a common mean. The most popular finance reading, keeping the 10% drift multiplicative for both baskets, gives a strictly positive in-expectation volatility/timing premium for B over the deterministic A, i.e. G, with the premium expectation-only and no a.s. dominance. The literal additive-vs-exponential reading gives A dominance in expectation. The martingale/same-mean statements B,C,D,F are false in levels; they hold only after drift discounting.
reflection_text.4:
The discussion remains split on how the 10 % “growth’’ is written in levels and on what is attainable in the 31st-year liquidation window.

Drift specification
* Basket A is described as “constant growth rate of 10 % each year … price is completely linear with no noise”. On a strict finance reading that is the deterministic geometric law P^A_t = P0 1.10^t a.s. The phrase “linear’’ is then used loosely for deterministic smooth. The alternative literal reading P^A_t = P0[1+0.10 t] a.s. is the one that makes the price literally linear in calendar time.
* Basket B is explicitly tied to an ARIMA-with-drift: ΔP^B_t = μ + ε_t, E[ε_t|F_{t-}] =0, constant autocovariance, 20 % weekly zero-mean moves. That is an additive drift in levels, E[P^B_t|F0]=P0+μ t, μ=0.10 P0 per year, i.e. a linear trend in levels, not P0 1.10^t. The innovations are stationary and zero mean once the known arithmetic drift is removed.

Martingale / stationary claims
* After drift adjustment both price processes are martingales in returns; in levels both are strict sub-martingales with positive drift. Statements B,C,D,F which assert a physical martingale, same average return or no excess return are false in levels. Basket A is degenerate so F is false; Basket B is not a martingale so D is false.
* Linearity of expectation kills a mean premium from any F-adapted liquidation schedule s_t≥0, ∫s_t dt=1: E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t] dt because E[ε_t|F_{t-}]=0. For a drifted sub-martingale E[P_τ]≤E[P_T] for τ≤T, the mean-maximising adapted rule is essentially τ=31 a.s. The ex-post running maximum M31=sup_[30,31] P^B_t satisfies E[M31]>E[P^B_31] but M31 is not an adapted payoff; a causal sell-on-up-move rule cannot realise the ex-post supremum in expectation.

Expected-value ordering under the wording-distinction reading
* With the intentional wording distinction constant proportional growth for A vs linear additive trend for B,
E[P^A_30]=P0 1.10^30≈17.45 P0,  E[P^B_30]=P0[1+0.10·30]=4.0 P0.
The 31st-year window adds the same additive μ to B and the compound 10 % to A. The zero-mean weekly shocks and any adapted timing can change dispersion but not the unconditional mean. Hence in unconditional expectation A strictly dominates B. Realised dominance fails both ways: σ>0 so a lucky path of B can finish above the deterministic A path, so E and H are false.

G camp and the multiplicative shorthand
* Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8 argue for the conventional finance shorthand E[P_{t+dt}|F_t]=P_t 1.10^{dt}. Under that shorthand E[P^A_t]=E[P^B_t]=P0 1.10^t on any fixed date. The 31st year then gives an American/look-back timing option: E[sup_[30,31] P^B_t]>E[P^B_31]. They claim an adapted gradual liquidation can approach the running maximum and that E[V^B_opt]>E[V^A]. The premium is in expectation only; realised B can still underperform A, so E and H remain false.
* Colleagues 12,5,7 object that the supremum is non-adapted. Under the physical drift the optional stopping theorem for the drift-adjusted martingale gives E[P_τ]≤E[P_T] and the expectation of any predictable stochastic integral with zero-mean noise is zero, so no unconditional mean premium is attainable by an adapted policy. That is the content of C, whose premise about a physical martingale is false even though the equality of the drift-adjusted mean is correct.

Unresolved tension
* The question explicitly differentiates “constant growth rate of 10 % each year’’ for A from “linear growth trend of 10 % each year … ARIMA with drift’’ for B, favouring the exponential-vs-additive reading and therefore the strict expected-value dominance of A.
* If the setter intended the common finance shorthand of a 10 % compound drift with noise for both baskets, the standard volatility/timing option argument gives G as the strongest true statement, with A/E/H and the martingale claims false. The private belief remains that the literal ARIMA wording is intended, so the additive-vs-compound reading and the strict expected-value dominance of A is the correct strongest true statement on the list, with the G argument relying on conflating E[sup] with the expectation of an adapted liquidation policy under the additive drift specification.

* Drift / level specification.
A is described as “constant growth rate of 10% each year … the stock price is completely linear with no noise.”  B is described as “linear growth trend of 10% each year (i.e., could be modeled by a non-seasonal ARIMA model with drift)” with 20% weekly moves, constant autocovariance, long-run volatility constant.

Then E[P^B_t]=P0[1+0.10 t]=P^A_t a.s., drift-adjusted returns are stationary zero-mean, and any F-adapted liquidation weight s_t≥0 satisfies E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t]dt.  The 31st-year window changes dispersion only.  Under this reading means are equal and the ex-post supremum M31=sup_{[30,31]}P^B_t is not an adapted payoff. The timing window cannot raise the unconditional mean of an adapted policy because E[P^B_τ]≤E[P^B_31] for τ≤31 and E[∫ s_t M_t dt]=0.  That yields strict expected-value dominance of A over B in expectation only.  Colleagues 3,4,7,8,9 argue this is the literal wording consequence and list A as the strongest true statement on that reading.
– Conventional multiplicative-drift finance reading: E[P_{t+dt}|F_t]=P_t 1.10^{dt} for both baskets, stationary zero-mean innovations after drift removal.  A is σ≡0, B is σ>0.  On any fixed calendar date E[P^A_t]=E[P^B_t]=P0 1.10^t.  The 31st-year window is an American/look-back timing option.  For a drifted sub-martingale with σ>0, E[ sup_{[30,31]}P^B_t |F30] > E[P^B_31|F30]=1.10 P^B_30.  An adapted sell-on-up-move rule can approximate the running maximum, giving a strictly positive in-expectation volatility/timing premium.  That is the G camp: Colleagues 10,11 and parts of 6,8, etc.  The premium is in expectation only; a bad realisation can still leave B below the certain A payoff, so E and H are false.

Both price processes are sub-martingales in levels under the physical measure with a 10% drift; they are not martingales.  Stationary returns do not imply a martingale in levels.  B,C,D,F are therefore widely rejected.  Colleague 12 and 5 stress the drift-adjusted martingale and optional stopping: E[P^B_τ]≤E[P^B_31], so the unconditional mean is maximised by liquidating as late as possible, and the supremum argument is an ex-post non-adapted payoff. The disagreement is precisely whether the supremum is attainable as an ex-ante expectation of an adapted policy.

Unresolved. The question’s wording is contradictory: “constant growth rate 10% per year” suggests compound, “price is completely linear with no noise” suggests arithmetic levels, and “linear growth trend … ARIMA with drift” strongly suggests additive levels for B. removed the weekly 20% innovations are stationary zero mean, but the
price level is not a martingale under P.  The drift-adjusted prices are
martingales; the levels are sub–martingales.

E[∫_{30}^{31}s_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt]

  =∫_{30}^{31}s_{t}P_{0}[1+0.10t]dt ,

because E[ε_{t}|{\cal F}_{t-}]=0.  For a bounded adapted stopping time
τ≤31

E[P^{B}_{τ}|{\cal F}_{0}]
   =E[P^{B}_{30}|{\cal F}_{0}]+μE[τ-30]
   ≤E[P^{B}_{31}|{\cal F}_{0}]

with equality only for τ≡31 a.s.  Linearity of expectation kills any
mean premium from timing: the zero mean weekly shocks contribute zero
to the unconditional mean of every admissible causal sales rule.
The 31st year window can change the distribution of the realised
liquidation value and it can raise E[sup_{[30,31]}P^{B}_{t}]>E[P^{B}_{31}],
but sup P^{B} is not an adapted payoff.  Selling early forfeits the
remaining positive expected arithmetic drift.

On the usual finance convention the deterministic basket is written
compound

P^{A,comp}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t} a.s.

In that conventional reading

E[P^{A,comp}_{30}]=P_{0}1.10^{30}\approx17.45P_{0}
   ≫P_{0}[1+3.0]=4.0P_{0}=E[P^{B}_{30}] .

Hence even with the optimal F-adapted liquidation in the 31st year

E[V^{B\,*}_{liq}]
  =E[P^{B}_{31}]
  =P_{0}[1+0.10·31]
  ≪P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A,comp}_{liq}] .

The dominance is in expectation only.  σ>0 so a realised path of B can
finish above the deterministic A path, so the a.s. dominances E and H
are false.  The price processes are sub–martingales in levels with a
10% drift, so the martingale statements B,C,D,F are false in levels.
With the literal ARIMA additive drift reading the deterministic

walk in unconditional expectation, i.e. the expected-value dominance

A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket B,

with the dominance being in expectation only.  On the multiplicative
drift convention E[P_{t+dt}|F_{t}]=P_{t}1.10^{dt} the two baskets share

8.text:
The 10 % has to be read as a multiplicative drift.  On the physical
measure

E[P_{t+dt}|F_{t}]=P_{t}\,(1+\mu dt),\qquad\mu =0.10,

so that on any pre-committed calendar date

E[P^{A}_{t}]=E[P^{B}_{t}]=P_{0}1.10^{t}

and after removing the known deterministic drift
$\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}1.10^{-t}$ is a martingale.  A is the $\sigma\equiv0$
degenerate case of that law, B is the strictly positive quadratic
variation case with the quoted 20 % weekly moves and constant long run
autocovariance.  In levels both are sub-martingales with the 10 % drift,
so the level martingale statements B,C,D,F are false.

The 31st year is an American/look-back timing option.  Put
$M_{31}=\sup_{t\in[30,31]}P^{B}_{t}$.  On every path
$M_{31}\ge P^{B}_{30}$ a.s. and $\sigma>0$ on $[30,31]$ makes the
inequality strict on a set of positive probability.  A gradual
sell-on-up-move rule can be made arbitrarily close to the running
maximum and by convexity

E[ M_{31}\mid F_{30}] > E[P^{B}_{31}\mid F_{30}]
      =1.10\,P^{B}_{30},

hence unconditionally

E[ V^{B}_{opt}] \ge E[M_{31}] > E[P^{B}_{31}]
        =P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[V^{A}] .

The deterministic basket has no timing premium,
$V^{A}_{31}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ a.s., whereas the adaptively timed
liquidation of the volatile drifted basket carries a strictly positive
in-expectation option value over the certain A payoff.  The premium is
in expectation only: a bad realisation of B can still finish below the
deterministic A payoff, so the a.s. dominances E and H are false.

That is the strictly positive volatility/timing premium

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

with the dominance being in expectation only.  On the literal additive
ARIMA-with-drift reading $E[P^{B}_{t}]=P_{0}[1+0.10t]$ the unconditional
mean of any $F$-adapted liquidation programme is the linear drift mean
and the two strategies have the same drift-adjusted mean; under the
compound reading of A this becomes the strict expected-value dominance
A of the deterministic compound basket over the additive-drift random
walk.  The martingale/identical-mean statements B–C are false in
levels; discounted by $1.10^{t}$ the drift-adjusted returns are the
stationary martingale differences referred to in the text.

2.text:
The 31st year window is the only thing that can change the comparison and
it does not change the unconditional mean of an admissible liquidation.

Put $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$ a.s. and, on the ARIMA-with-drift reading
that the text invites,

$P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t+W_{t},\qquad E[W_{t}|{\cal F}_{0}]=0,$

$E[P^{B}_{t+s}|{\cal F}_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}+0.10P_{0}s$, 
$E[P^{B}_{t}|{\cal F}_{0}]=P_{0}[1+0.10t]$.

After removing the known deterministic $0.10$ arithmetic drift the weekly
innovations are stationary, zero mean and long-run autocovariance is
constant.  Drift discounted, $P^{A,\mu}_{t}$ and $P^{B,\mu}_{t}$ are
martingales and $A$ is the $\sigma\equiv0$ degenerate case of the same
drifted law.  In levels both prices are strictly positive sub-martingales
with the $10\%$ p.a. arithmetic drift; the “martingale’’ language in B–C
is the usual drift-adjusted shorthand for return stationarity.

Let $s_{t}\ge0$, $\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}dt=1$, be an $F$-adapted liquidation
weight and $\tau\in[30,31]$ an $F$-stopping time.  Predictability gives

$E\Big[\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt\Big]
   =\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}E[P^{B}_{t}]dt
   =\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}P_{0}[1+0.10t]dt$,

and $E[s_{t}W_{t}]=0$ for every predictable $s_{t}$.  For the drifted
sub-martingale

$E[P^{B}_{\tau}|{\cal F}_{0}]
   =E[P^{B}_{30}|{\cal F}_{0}]+0.10P_{0}E[\tau-30]
   \le E[P^{B}_{31}|{\cal F}_{0}]$,

with equality only for $\tau\equiv31$ a.s.  Hence the zero-mean $20\%$
weekly moves are pure dispersion around the common drifted mean.  The
ex-post running maximum $M_{31}=\sup_{t\in[30,31]}P^{B}_{t}$ satisfies
$E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$ but $M_{31}$ is not an $F$-adapted payoff; a
causal sell-on-up-move rule forfeits the remaining positive drift and
$E[\int s_{t}W_{t}dt]=0$.

Consequently on the literal additive/linear reading that the text
“price is completely linear with no noise’’ and “ARIMA…with drift’’ calls
for

$E[V^{B}_{\rm liq}]=E[V^{A}_{\rm liq}]
      =P_{0}[1+0.10\cdot31]$

in the limit of liquidation at the end of the 31st year; the 31st year
window changes the distribution of the realised liquidation value, it
raises dispersion and $E[\sup P^{B}_{t}]>E[P^{B}_{t}]$ ex post, but it
does not raise the unconditional mean of any admissible causal
programme.  That is the stationary-return/martingale-after-drift content
of the equal-mean statement.  In particular $E$ and $H$ are false in
realisation, $A$ and $G$ are false in unconditional mean under the
additive linear reading, and the price processes are sub-martingales in
levels so the level-martingale claims $B,D,F$ are false in levels.  The
statement that captures the equal unconditional mean of the two
strategies is the C statement, the average-return version being the
B statement.

9.text:
The 31st year liquidation is an $ {\cal F}$-adapted control.  Write for B

$P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+\mu t+M_{t},\qquad \mu =0.10P_{0}{\rm yr^{-1}},\;E[dM_{t}|{\cal F}_{t-}]=0,$

and for the deterministic basket, on the literal wording of the problem,

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+\mu t\;a.s.$

so that after removal of the known $10\%$ arithmetic drift

$\widetilde P_{t}=P_{t}1_{t}^{-1}$ 

is a martingale and the return innovations are stationary zero mean with
constant long run autocovariance.  In levels both prices are strict
sub-martingales with the same arithmetic drift,

$E\!\left[P^{B}_{t+s}|{\cal F}_{t}\right]=P^{B}_{t}+\mu s,\qquad 
E\!\left[P^{B}_{t}|{\cal F}_{0}\right]=P_{0}+\mu t=P^{A}_{t},$

i.e. on any fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=E[P^{A}_{t}]=P_{0}[1+0.10t].$

Let $0\le L_{t}\le1$, $L_{30}=0$, $L_{31}=1$, be the adapted cumulative
fraction sold on $[30,31]$ and put $s_{t}=dL_{t}/dt$.  Integration by
parts

$V(L)=\int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}dL_{t}=P^{B}_{31}-\int_{30}^{31}L_{t}dP^{B}_{t}$

gives

$E[V(L)|{\cal F}_{30}]=E[P^{B}_{31}|{\cal F}_{30}]-\mu
E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}L_{t}dt\Big|{\cal F}_{30}\right]
\le E[P^{B}_{31}|{\cal F}_{30}]$

with equality iff $L_{t}\equiv0$ on $[30,31)$ a.s., i.e. $\tau\equiv31$.
Since $E[\int L_{t}dM_{t}]=0$ for a predictable $L$,

$E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}P^{B}_{t}dt\right]
 =\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}E[P^{B}_{t}]dt,$

so the zero mean weekly $20\%$ shocks contribute zero to the
unconditional mean of any causal sales rule.  The $31^{\rm st}$ year
window therefore changes the dispersion of the realised liquidation
value and

$E\!\left[\sup_{t\in[30,31]}P^{B}_{t}\right]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$

but $\sup_{[30,31]}P^{B}_{t}$ is not an $ {\cal F}$-adapted payoff.  A
causal gradual sell-on-up-move rule forfeits the remaining positive
arithmetic drift and

$E[P^{B}_{\tau}] \le E[P^{B}_{31}]$

for every bounded adapted $\tau\le31$, with equality only for the
terminal rule.  The high variance of B is pure risk around the common
drifted mean.

Hence with the additive ARIMA-drift reading forced by “linear growth
trend … ARIMA with drift’’ and by “price is completely linear with no
noise’’ for A, the two strategies have the same long run average
liquidation value.  In drift-adjusted terms the return innovations are
stationary and $1.10^{-t}P_{t}$ is a martingale, i.e. the stationary-return
statement in the prompt, and the unconditional mean of any admissible
liquidation programme is the common drifted forward value

$E[V^{B}_{liq}]=E[V^{A}_{liq}]=\int_{30}^{31}s_{t}\!\left(P_{0}+\mu t\right)dt,$

maximised by essentially terminal liquidation.  The volatility of B
raises $E[\sup P^{B}]$ and the pathwise distribution of the realised
payoff but it does not raise $E[\,\cdot\,]$; the in-expectation
‘volatility/timing’ premium claimed for G is the ex-post supremum
confused with the ex-ante expectation of an adapted liquidation policy.
On the conventional multiplicative-drift finance convention
$E[P_{t+dt}|{\cal F}_{t}]=1.10^{dt}P_{t}$ the same calculation gives
$E[P^{A}_{t}]=P_{0}1.10^{t}=E[P^{B}_{t}]$ on a fixed date and the
additive ARIMA reading $E[P^{B}_{t}]=P_{0}[1+0.10t]$ makes the
deterministic compound basket strictly dominate B in expectation, i.e.
the A ordering.  With the literal linear-in-levels wording of the
question the equality of the unconditional means is the content of C,
and E and H are impossible because $\sigma>0$ allows a realised B path
to finish above the deterministic A path. ∎

* B : “a linear growth trend of 10 % each year … could be modelled by a
non-seasonal ARIMA model with drift’’

P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+μt+M_{t},  E[M_{t}|F_{0}]=0,
E[P^{B}_{t+Δ}|F_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}+μΔ, 
E[P^{B}_{t}|F_{0}]=P_{0}+μt=P_{0}[1+0.10t] .

After the known deterministic arithmetic drift μt is removed the
weekly innovations are stationary zero mean with constant long run
autocovariance.  Discounting by the deterministic drift,

\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}1.10^{-t}

the drift-adjusted price is a martingale and the two baskets are the
σ≡0 degenerate case and the σ>0 case of the same drifted law.  On any

E[P^{A}_{t}] = E[P^{B}_{t}] = P_{0}[1+0.10t] .

and τ≤31 an F-stopping time.  With P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+μt+M_{t} and M a

+E[∫s_{t}M_{t}dt]=∫_{30}^{31}s_{t}[P_{0}+μt]dt ,

E[P^{B}_{τ}|F_{0}]=E[P^{B}_{30}|F_{0}]+μE[τ-30]≤E[P^{B}_{31}|F_{0}]

with equality only for τ≡31 a.s.  The predictable stochastic integral

mean, so the 20 % weekly moves change dispersion only.  In particular
E[sup_{30≤t≤31}P^{B}_{t}]>E[P^{B}_{31}] is true for the non-adapted
ex-post supremum, but the supremum is not an admissible causal payoff.
Selling on up-moves forfeits the remaining positive arithmetic drift and
the expectation of the noise is zero for every adapted rule.

Hence an adapted liquidation over the 31st year cannot raise the
unconditional mean.  The two strategies share the same drifted forward
mean, the volatile basket being pure risk around the common arithmetic
10 % mean.  The high variance of B is dispersion, not a mean premium.
In levels the prices are positive sub-martingales with the 10 % arithmetic
drift; after drift discounting they are martingales and the return
innovations are stationary.  That is the content of the stationary-return
/ martingale-after-drift statement, viz. the equality of the unconditional
expected liquidation values.

The necessary a.s. dominances E and H are false and the strict

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The drift wording is the whole fight and the round-3 public set splits three ways: literal ARIMA-additive vs conventional multiplicative-drift finance vs drift-adjusted martingale equality.

Drift specification
* Basket A: “constant growth rate of 10% each year … price is completely linear with no noise”. On a finance reading that is the deterministic geometric law P^A_t = P0 1.10^t a.s. The phrase “linear” is used loosely for deterministic smooth. Literal linear-in-levels reading would be P0[1+0.10 t] a.s.
* Basket B: explicitly “linear growth trend of 10% each year … ARIMA with drift”. That is additive in levels ΔP^B_t = μ+ε_t, E[ε_t|F_{t-}] =0, μ =0.10 P0 per year, so E[P^B_t|F0]=P0+μt = P0[1+0.10 t], a linear trend in levels with stationary zero-mean weekly shocks, 20% weekly moves, constant long-run autocovariance. After drift removal the increments are stationary; in levels P^B is a strict sub-martingale with arithmetic drift.

Martingale / stationary claims
* In levels both processes are sub-martingales with positive drift, not physical martingales. Drift-adjusted prices \tilde P_t = P_t 1.10^{-t} are martingales. Statements B,C,D,F that assert a physical martingale, same average return, no excess return, etc., are false in levels. Basket A is degenerate, so F is false; Basket B is not a martingale so D is false.
* For any F-adapted liquidation weight s_t≥0, ∫s_t dt=1, or adapted stopping τ∈[30,31],
E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t] dt because E[ε_t|F_{t-}]=0. Linearity of expectation kills a mean premium from timing. For arithmetic drift E[P_τ] ≤ E[P_T] with equality only τ=31 a.s., so expectation-maximising adapted rule is essentially sell at end of window. E[sup_[30,31] P^B_t] > E[P^B_31] is true for the ex-post supremum, but sup is not an adapted payoff; a causal sell-on-up-move rule cannot realise the future running maximum in expectation and selling early forfeits remaining positive expected drift.

Expected-value ordering under the intentional wording distinction
* With constant proportional growth for A vs linear additive trend for B,
E[P^A_30]=P0 1.10^30≈17.45 P0, E[P^B_30]=P0[1+0.10·30]=4.0 P0.
The 31st-year window adds the same additive μ to B and compound 10% to A. Zero-mean weekly shocks and any adapted timing change dispersion but not the unconditional mean. Realised dominance fails both ways because σ>0, so E and H are false.
* Hence under the literal ARIMA-additive reading the strongest true statement on the list is A. The strategy of choosing basket A has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket B, dominance in expectation only.

G camp and multiplicative shorthand
* Colleagues 11,2,3,4,6,8 argue for conventional finance shorthand E[P_{t+dt}|F_t]=P_t 1.10^{dt}. Under that shorthand E[P^A_t]=E[P^B_t]=P0 1.10^t on any fixed date. The 31st-year timing option then gives E[sup_[30,31] P^B_t]>E[P^B_31] and they claim an adapted gradual liquidation can approach the running maximum, giving G: E[V^B_opt]>E[V^A]. The premium is in expectation only; realised B can still underperform A, so E/H remain false.
* Colleagues 5,7,9 argue the drift-adjusted martingale view leading to C: unconditional expected liquidation value is the same for both, liquidation timing is mean-preserving. That is the equal-mean statement under the additive linear-in-levels reading of both baskets.
* Colleagues 1,10,12,4 now explicitly endorse the literal wording distinction and the strict expected-value dominance A, noting that the G premium is a confusion of ex-post supremum with ex-ante expectation of an adapted policy under the additive drift specification.

Unresolved tension
* The question explicitly differentiates “constant growth rate” for A from “linear growth trend … ARIMA with drift” for B, favouring exponential-vs-additive reading and therefore strict expected-value dominance of A.
* If the setter intended the common finance shorthand of 10% compound drift with noise for both, the standard volatility/timing option argument gives G as the strongest true statement, with A/E/H and the martingale claims false.
Private belief remains that the literal ARIMA wording is intended, so the additive-vs-compound reading and the strict expected-value dominance of A is the correct strongest true statement on the list, with G relying on conflating E[sup] with the expectation of an adapted liquidation policy under the additive drift specification.

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation is now three-way over how the 10% is written and whether the 31st-year window can raise the ex-ante mean.

Drift / level specification.

The 20 % weekly moves are stationary zero-mean innovations with constant long-run autocovariance. After removing the known deterministic arithmetic drift the increments are stationary zero mean.

A is described as “constant growth rate of 10 % each year … stock price is completely linear with no noise”. On a literal levels reading that is
P^A_t = P0+0.10 P0 t = P0[1+0.10 t] a.s.
Discounting by the deterministic drift \tilde P_t = P_t - μt is a martingale; in levels both prices are strictly positive sub-martingales with a 10 % arithmetic drift, so the level-martingale claims B,D,F are false in levels.

For an F-adapted weight s_t≥0, ∫_{30}^{31}s_t dt=1, or an adapted stopping τ∈[30,31],
E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t] dt,
E[P^B_τ]=E[P^B_30]+μE[τ-30] ≤ E[P^B_31],
with equality only for τ≡31 a.s. The predictable stochastic integral with the zero-mean martingale part has zero unconditional mean, so the 20 % weekly shocks contribute zero to the unconditional mean of every causal liquidation programme. The 31st-year window changes dispersion and the pathwise distribution, and
E[sup_{[30,31]}P^B_t] > E[P^B_31],
but sup P^B is not an adapted payoff. A causal sell-on-up-move rule forfeits the remaining positive expected arithmetic drift; the expectation of the noise remains zero.

Hence on the literal linear-in-levels reading
E[P^A_t]=E[P^B_t]=P0[1+0.10 t]
and the unconditional expected liquidation value of any admissible adapted programme is the common drifted forward value. The extra variance of B is pure risk around that common mean, no mean premium from timing. That is the content of C, the equality of unconditional expected liquidation values, with E and H false because σ>0 allows a realised B path to finish above the deterministic A path.

Compound/exponential finance reading.  
If “10 % p.a. growth’’ is read in the conventional multiplicative finance shorthand
E[P_{t+dt}|F_t]=1.10^{dt}P_t,
then on a fixed calendar date
E[P^A_t]=E[P^B_t]=P0 1.10^t.
A is the σ≡0 degenerate case of the same drifted law, B is a strictly positive sub-martingale with σ>0. The 31st year is an American/look-back timing privilege. With the usual M_{31}=sup_{[30,31]}P^B_t,
E[M_{31}|F_{30}] > E[P^B_{31}|F_{30}] =1.10 P^B_{30},
so the ex-post supremum has a strictly positive look-back/volatility option value. Under the conventional “maximise realised liquidation value’’ reading the attainable ex-ante mean with an adapted gradual liquidation can be made to approach E[M_{31}], giving
E[V^B_opt] > P0 1.10^{31}=E[V^A].
The premium is in expectation only; a bad draw can put realised V^B below V^A, so E and H remain false and the processes remain sub-martingales in levels, so B,C,D,F remain false in levels. This is the G statement.

Exponential-A vs additive-B mismatch.  
If A is kept as the textbook compound
P^A_t = P0 1.10^t a.s.
while B is kept as the ARIMA additive drift
E[P^B_t]=P0[1+0.10 t],
then
E[P^B_30]=4.0 P0 ≪ P^A_30≈17.45 P0,
and E[P^B_31]≪P^A_31. The deterministic exponential basket strictly dominates the additive-drift random walk in unconditional expectation, i.e. A. The dominance is in expectation only; σ>0 allows a realised B path to finish above A, so E and H are false.

Current round evidence. Colleagues 1,10,12,4,6 push the exponential-vs-additive reading to A; colleagues 2,3,5,7,9 push the literal linear-in-levels equal-mean reading to C; colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8 push the conventional multiplicative drift with timing option to G. The martingale/equal-mean claims B,C,D,F are consistently rejected in levels because the 10 % drift makes prices sub-martingales, and the necessary pathwise dominances E,H are consistently rejected. The choice between A/C/G therefore remains entirely a matter of textual parsing of “constant growth rate… price completely linear’’ for A versus “linear growth trend … ARIMA with drift’’ for B, and of whether the 31st-year liquidation is required to be strictly F-adapted, in which case the unconditional mean cannot be raised, or is allowed to be evaluated as an ex-post supremum/look-back option.

Unresolved: whether the exam intends the literal linear-in-levels ARIMA reading giving equal unconditional means C, or the conventional multiplicative drift reading giving a volatility/timing option premium G, or the mixed exponential-A / additive-B reading giving strict expected dominance A.

reflection_text.2:
The discussion remains centred on the drift specification and on what is attainable with an F-adapted liquidation over [30,31].

* Drift specification. Basket A is described as “constant growth rate of 10% each year … price is completely linear with no noise”. Basket B is described as a “linear growth trend of 10% each year i.e. a non-seasonal ARIMA with drift” with stationary zero-mean 20% weekly shocks and constant long-run autocovariance. On a literal level reading an ARIMA-with-drift is additive in levels
ΔP^B_t = μ+ε_t ,  E[ε_t|F_{t-}]=0 , μ=0.10 P0 yr^{-1}
so E[P^B_t|F0]=P0+μt = P0[1+0.10t]. The phrase “price is completely linear with no noise’’ for A is most naturally read as the same arithmetic line P^A_t = P0+μt a.s., i.e. the σ≡0 degenerate case of the same drifted law. Under this literal linear-in-levels reading after removing the known deterministic arithmetic drift the increments are stationary zero-mean, P_t 1.10^{-t} is the usual drift-adjusted martingale shorthand and in levels both prices are strictly positive sub-martingales with a 10% arithmetic drift, not physical martingales.

If the conventional finance shorthand E[P_{t+dt}|F_t]=P_t1.10^{dt} is imposed for both baskets, then E[P_t]=P0 1.10^t on any fixed date and A is the σ≡0 degenerate case of the same compound drifted law. That is the reading used for the G camp.

* Adapted liquidation vs ex-post supremum. For an F-adapted liquidation weight s_t≥0, ∫ s_t dt=1, or an adapted stopping τ∈[30,31], write P^B_t = P0+μt+M_t with M a zero-mean martingale. Predictability gives
E[∫ s_t P^B_t dt]=∫ s_t E[P^B_t]dt,  E[∫ s_t M_t dt]=0,
and for a stopping time E[P^B_τ]=E[P^B_30]+μ E[τ-30] ≤ E[P^B_31] with equality only for τ≡31 a.s. Optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale therefore preserves the unconditional mean; a causal sell-on-up-move rule forfeits remaining positive expected arithmetic drift and the expectation of the zero-mean shocks is zero for every admissible causal schedule.

It is true pathwise that M31 = sup_{t∈[30,31]}P^B_t ≥ P^B_30 a.s. and E[M31]>E[P^B_31] for σ>0. M31 is not an adapted payoff. The “volatility/timing premium’’ is an ex-post supremum/look-back effect, not an increase in the ex-ante expectation of an admissible F-adapted programme. That distinction is the core error in the G argument presented by Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8.
